cardiac-cycle.name: The cardiac cycle
cardiac-cycle.summary: One heartbeat is a sequence of filling and ejection: diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, and systole, when they contract and pump.
body: Each cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds at rest. During diastole the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and blood flows passively from the atria into the ventricles; the atria then contract to add the final fifth. Ventricular systole begins as pressure rises, the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut (the first heart sound, 'lub'), and once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure the aortic and pulmonary valves open and blood is ejected.

As the ventricles relax, pressure falls, the aortic and pulmonary valves close (the second heart sound, 'dub') and the cycle repeats. The valves make flow one-way; the papillary muscles and chordae tendineae stop the mitral and tricuspid leaflets bulging back into the atria.
The fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected, the ejection fraction, is normally 55 to 70% and is the everyday measure of how well the left ventricle pumps.

Each half of the cycle begins with a phase in which the ventricle changes pressure but not volume. In isovolumetric contraction, the first phase of systole, the rising pressure slams the atrioventricular valves shut but has not yet opened the semilunar valves, so no blood leaves; ejection follows once ventricular pressure exceeds that in the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Diastole likewise opens with isovolumic relaxation, when all four valves are closed and pressure falls until the atrioventricular valves reopen. The ventricle never empties completely: the volume left after ejection is the end-systolic volume, and stroke volume is the difference between the end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes. The two heart sounds mark the valve closures: S1 (lub) is the atrioventricular valves shutting at the start of systole and S2 (dub) is the semilunar valves shutting at the start of diastole, which is why a murmur heard between S1 and S2 arises during ejection.

Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, and stroke volume depends on three things: preload, the stretch on the ventricle before it contracts (another expression of end-diastolic volume, set by filling time and venous return); contractility, the force of the contraction itself, which the autonomic nerves and hormones such as adrenaline increase; and afterload, the pressure the ventricle must overcome to open the semilunar valves, which rises with high blood pressure. In exercise, heart rate and stroke volume both increase, so output rises several-fold in a healthy young adult; in heart failure the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, either because the weakened ventricle ejects a reduced fraction or because a stiff ventricle fills poorly while ejecting a preserved fraction, the latter driven mainly by high blood pressure and other conditions that make the heart work harder.

The cycle is assessed non-invasively with echocardiography, which uses sound waves to produce moving images showing the size and shape of the heart, how well it is pumping and how the valves open and close; it is the test that produces the ejection fraction and classifies heart failure as reduced or preserved. Blood levels of brain natriuretic peptide, released by stretched ventricles, rise in heart failure, and cardiac MRI, CT or nuclear scans give further measures of pumping when needed. Faulty valves, an irregular rhythm and inherited or congenital heart disease are among the structural causes that these tests uncover.

heart-rate.name: Heart rate
heart-rate.summary: How often the heart beats, set by the sinoatrial node and adjusted second by second by the autonomic nervous system and hormones.
body: The sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium fires spontaneously about 100 times a minute if left alone. At rest the vagus nerve slows it to a typical 60 to 100 beats per minute; sympathetic nerves and adrenaline speed it up during exercise, fear or fever.

Trained athletes often have resting rates in the 40s because each beat pumps more blood. Rates persistently above 100 (tachycardia) or below 60 (bradycardia) are only abnormal in context: a rate of 45 in a marathon runner is normal, in a fainting older adult it may signal heart block.
Heart rate is one of the vital signs and is measured at the radial pulse, on an ECG, or by pulse oximeters and wearables.

Each beat begins as an electrical signal in the pacemaker cells of the sinoatrial node in the right atrium. The signal spreads first through the atria, which contract and push blood into the ventricles, and then through the ventricles, which contract and pump blood out of the heart; the closing of the aortic and pulmonary valves after ventricular ejection produces the second heart sound. Nerve signals and hormones set how fast and how hard this sequence repeats. During exercise the heart rate rises to carry more oxygen to the working muscles, and a trained heart, being larger, can deliver the same blood flow with fewer beats.

Checking the pulse by hand remains a basic clinical skill. The NHS describes finding it on the inside of the wrist at the base of the thumb, or at the side of the neck beside the windpipe, pressing lightly with the index and middle fingers rather than the thumb, which has a pulse of its own. For a resting value the person sits quietly for a few minutes first and avoids smoking or caffeine beforehand; beats are counted over a full minute, or over half a minute and doubled. Feeling whether the beats arrive at even intervals checks the rhythm as well as the rate: occasional skipped beats are common, but a persistently irregular pulse can be a sign of atrial fibrillation and is checked with an ECG.

Rate and rhythm together are what clinicians interpret. Fitter people rest at lower rates, so a slow pulse in someone who feels well is rarely a concern, whereas a persistently fast or slow resting pulse in someone who feels unwell, or an irregular one, prompts medical review. Fever, pain, dehydration, blood loss, anaemia and an overactive thyroid all raise the resting rate; heart block, hypothyroidism and some medicines such as beta blockers lower it.

blood-pressure.name: Blood pressure
blood-pressure.summary: The pressure blood exerts on artery walls: systolic at the peak of ejection, diastolic between beats.
body: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps each minute (cardiac output) and how hard it is to push that blood through the small arteries (peripheral resistance). The elastic aorta smooths the pulse; the muscular arterioles set resistance and are the main site of control.

Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch report pressure to the brainstem, which adjusts heart rate and vessel tone within seconds. Over hours and days the kidneys take over, adjusting salt and water excretion through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic in millimetres of mercury. Values around 120/80 mmHg are typical; sustained readings of 140/90 mmHg or more define hypertension in most guidelines.

Blood pressure is a form of hydrostatic pressure: the force the blood exerts on the walls of the vessels and the chambers of the heart. Two derived numbers matter clinically. Pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic, reflects how much the arteries are stretched by each ejection; it widens harmlessly after strenuous exercise but a persistently wide pulse pressure can indicate stiff or resistant arteries. Mean arterial pressure is the average pressure across the cycle and is the pressure that actually drives blood into the tissues. Five variables govern pressure and flow in the systemic circulation: cardiac output, the compliance of the vessels, the blood volume, the viscosity of the blood, and the length and diameter of the vessels. Of these, arteriolar diameter is the most responsive: the arterioles have such narrow lumens that a slight dilation greatly lowers resistance and a slight constriction greatly raises it, which is why they are called resistance vessels. Constriction of veins also raises pressure within them and helps return blood to the heart.

Measurement uses a cuff on the upper arm. The traditional sphygmomanometer combines a cuff, a pump, a dial and a stethoscope: the cuff is inflated until it stops the flow, then slowly released, and the first sound heard through the stethoscope (the first Korotkoff sound) marks the systolic pressure while the point at which the sounds disappear marks the diastolic. Automatic devices sense the pulse through the cuff and show both numbers on a digital display. For a reliable reading the person rests for several minutes, sits with the back supported and legs uncrossed, keeps the arm supported at heart level and free of tight clothing, and stays still and silent; readings are repeated because the first is often highest.

A single clinic reading is only a snapshot. Pressure rises with exercise, pain, cold, a full bladder and anxiety, and readings taken in a clinic can run higher than at home, the so-called white coat effect. For this reason diagnosis is usually confirmed with home monitoring using a validated upper-arm device, or with ambulatory monitoring, in which a portable cuff records pressure automatically through the day and night. Persistently raised pressure strains the heart, arteries, kidneys and brain and is a major treatable risk factor for stroke and heart attack, while an abrupt fall in pressure, as in haemorrhage or sepsis, deprives the organs of flow.

cardiac-output.name: Cardiac output
cardiac-output.summary: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, about five litres at rest.
body: Stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat, rises when the ventricle fills more (the Frank-Starling mechanism: a more stretched muscle contracts harder), when contractility increases under sympathetic drive, and when the resistance it pumps against falls.

During hard exercise cardiac output can reach 20 to 25 litres per minute in a fit adult, mostly through a faster rate and a larger stroke volume, while blood is redirected from the gut and kidneys to the muscles.
A failing heart cannot raise its output to meet demand; the resulting breathlessness on exertion and fluid retention are the hallmarks of heart failure.

Stroke volume itself is set by three things clinicians name separately: preload, the volume of blood returning to fill the ventricle at the end of diastole; afterload, the pressure the left ventricle must push against to open the aortic valve; and contractility, the intrinsic strength of the muscle's squeeze, which also depends on heart size, fitness and sex. The nervous system and hormones adjust how fast and how hard the heart beats, and changes in cardiac output from its resting baseline track the body's total oxygen requirement almost directly, so output climbs with fever, anxiety or exertion and falls during sleep.

Cardiac output is rarely measured directly in everyday care. Stroke volume is usually estimated by echocardiography as the difference between the ventricle's end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, then multiplied by the heart rate. In intensive care and cardiac catheterisation laboratories the Fick principle is used instead: the output is calculated from the body's oxygen uptake and the difference in oxygen content between arterial and mixed venous blood, although this can underestimate tissue consumption when the lungs themselves use a lot of oxygen. Because a large person needs more flow than a small one, the result is often normalised to body surface area as the cardiac index; cardiac output on its own cannot reliably judge how well the heart is performing.

In disease the relationship between demand and output breaks down. A dilated, failing ventricle keeps output up at first through neurohormonal compensation, with sympathetic activation raising heart rate and contractility, but these same responses eventually worsen the strain. Large blood loss, severe valve disease and shock all lower stroke volume, and when disease or injury weakens the heart the organs no longer receive enough blood to work normally.

cardiac-conduction.name: Electrical conduction of the heart
cardiac-conduction.summary: A wiring system of specialised muscle cells spreads each heartbeat from the sinoatrial node through the atria, the atrioventricular node and the bundle branches to the ventricles.
body: The impulse starts in the sinoatrial node, sweeps across both atria (the P wave of the ECG) and reaches the atrioventricular node, which delays it for about a tenth of a second so the atria finish emptying. It then races down the bundle of His and the right and left bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres, depolarising the ventricles from the apex upward (the QRS complex). Recovery of the ventricles produces the T wave.

Because the wave follows a fixed path, its timing on an ECG reveals blocks (a long PR interval or a bundle branch block), extra pathways and the chaotic atrial activity of atrial fibrillation. Damaged muscle after a heart attack changes the shape of the QRS and ST segments.
Pacemakers replace a failing sinoatrial node or a blocked atrioventricular node; ablation destroys tissue that generates abnormal rhythms.

Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic: unlike skeletal or smooth muscle it generates its own electrical signal at a set rate. Two kinds of cell share the work. Conductive cells, a small minority, set the rate and spread the impulse; contractile cells do the pumping. The pacemaker cells of the sinoatrial node never rest at a stable voltage: a slow inward leak of sodium (the prepotential) drifts the membrane toward threshold, rapid calcium entry then fires the action potential and potassium exit resets it, so the node fires rhythmically without any external command. The heart nonetheless receives neural and endocrine input: sympathetic nerves and adrenaline steepen the prepotential and speed the rate during exercise, stress or fever, while parasympathetic (vagal) activity slows it at rest and in sleep, which is why heart rate is a sensitive barometer of the body's state.

Disorders fall into two groups. In arrhythmias the heart beats too fast (tachycardia), too slowly (bradycardia) or irregularly, because abnormal extra signals arise, signals are blocked or slowed, or they travel along new pathways; many are harmless, but atrial fibrillation, in which the atria beat chaotically and out of step with the ventricles, is the commonest serious type, and ventricular fibrillation stops effective pumping and causes sudden death unless a shock is delivered immediately. In conduction disorders (heart block) the signal is not produced properly or does not travel through the heart as it should; in a bundle branch block the signal travels more slowly down one side than the other. Inherited channel disorders such as long QT syndrome arise from ion channels that work poorly or are too few, and are unmasked by low potassium, magnesium or calcium and by medicines including some antibiotics and antidepressants.

The electrocardiogram remains the central test because it records the electrical activity directly. Intermittent symptoms may need several ECGs over days or weeks or a Holter monitor worn continuously; an exercise stress test shows how the rhythm behaves when the heart is working hard; blood tests check electrolytes and thyroid hormone, which alter conduction; an echocardiogram looks at the heart's size and structure, since damage from high blood pressure or coronary disease underlies many arrhythmias.

circulation.name: Circulation
circulation.summary: Two circuits in series: the pulmonary circulation loads blood with oxygen in the lungs, the systemic circulation delivers it to every organ.
body: The right heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary arteries into the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and unloads carbon dioxide before returning through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left heart pumps it into the aorta and on through arteries, arterioles and capillaries, where exchange with the tissues happens, then back through venules and veins to the right atrium.

Pressure falls along the way: from about 120 mmHg in the aorta to a few mmHg in the great veins. Veins hold about two thirds of the blood volume at any moment and return it to the heart with the help of valves, the muscle pump of the legs and the suction of breathing.
Special circuits exist: the hepatic portal system carries gut blood through the liver first, and the coronary circulation supplies the heart muscle itself during diastole.

Tracing the route in detail: blood low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide reaches the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, which drains the heart muscle itself. The right ventricle ejects it into the pulmonary trunk, past the pulmonary semilunar valve that stops it falling back during diastole; the trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries, the only arteries in the adult body carrying deoxygenated blood. Oxygen-rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and the left ventricle pumps it into the aorta, which has an ascending part giving off the coronary arteries, an arch supplying the head and arms, and a descending part with thoracic and abdominal segments supplying everything else. Four chambers working in pairs and four valves keep the flow in one direction.

Control of where the blood goes lies in the arterioles. Their narrow lumens make them the resistance vessels: a slight dilation greatly increases the flow to an organ and a slight constriction greatly reduces it, so during exercise the arterioles of the working muscles open while those of the gut and kidneys narrow, and cardiac output rises severalfold to feed the muscles. Constriction of veins raises the pressure within them and helps return blood to the heart, which matters when standing up or after blood loss. The pulse felt at the wrist is the expansion and recoil of an artery with each beat and so reflects the heartbeat.

Circulation is assessed by the pulse, the blood pressure measured with an arm cuff, the warmth and colour of the skin and how quickly it refills after pressure, and the urine output, which falls early when organs are underperfused. If disease or injury weakens the heart the organs no longer receive enough blood to work normally: in heart failure fluid backs up into the lungs and legs, in shock the skin becomes cool and mottled and the brain and kidneys fail, and in peripheral arterial disease narrowed leg arteries cause pain on walking. Echocardiography, Doppler ultrasound of the vessels and angiography show where in the circuit the problem lies.

breathing.name: Breathing (ventilation)
breathing.summary: Air moves in and out because muscles change the volume of the chest: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge it for inspiration; relaxation and elastic recoil empty it.
body: When the diaphragm contracts its dome flattens and the ribs swing up and out, lowering pressure inside the chest below atmospheric pressure so air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall recoil. Forced breathing recruits the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals to push air out, and the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids to pull the ribs up.

The rhythm is generated in the medulla and pons and adjusted by chemoreceptors that sense carbon dioxide and, to a lesser extent, oxygen. A rising carbon dioxide level is the strongest normal drive to breathe.
Airway resistance matters: narrowing the bronchi even slightly, as in asthma, greatly increases the work of breathing because resistance rises with the fourth power of the reduction in radius.

The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle beneath the lungs. When it tightens, the dome flattens downward and the chest cavity enlarges; the muscles between the ribs help by lifting the rib cage. The lungs expand to fill the extra space and air is drawn in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe and through the branching bronchial tubes to the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where exchange happens. Their walls are extremely thin and each is wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, so oxygen crosses into the blood and is bound by haemoglobin in red cells while carbon dioxide leaves the blood to be breathed out. Breathing out is normally passive: the diaphragm and rib muscles relax, the cavity shrinks and the elastic lungs recoil to push the air out, with the abdominal muscles joining in only during hard exercise, coughing or forced exhalation.

The volume of each breath and the rate together set the ventilation, and both rise during exercise so that the extra carbon dioxide produced by the muscles is removed as fast as it is made; at rest the chemoreceptor response to carbon dioxide keeps the level remarkably constant. Residual air that stays in the lungs after the deepest expiration prevents the alveoli from collapsing between breaths, so each breath only has to top up a reservoir rather than inflate the lungs from empty.

Breathing is assessed first by watching: rate, depth, use of the neck and shoulder muscles, and whether the person can speak in full sentences. Spirometry measures how much air can be blown out and how fast, and shows the narrowed airways of asthma or COPD as slow emptying; pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases show whether the exchange is keeping oxygen up and carbon dioxide down. Disorders of the pump, such as a weak diaphragm in neuromuscular disease, a stiff chest wall or depressed respiratory drive from opioids, reduce ventilation even when the lungs themselves are healthy, and the first sign is a rising carbon dioxide level.

gas-exchange.name: Gas exchange
gas-exchange.summary: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin wall between alveoli and capillaries by diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressure.
body: The lungs contain about 300 million alveoli with a combined surface close to the size of a tennis court, separated from blood by a membrane under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into the blood because its partial pressure in alveolar air (about 100 mmHg) exceeds that in returning venous blood (about 40 mmHg); carbon dioxide moves the other way down a smaller gradient because it diffuses twenty times more readily.

Efficient exchange needs ventilation and blood flow to be matched. Blood sent to unventilated alveoli (as in pneumonia) is not oxygenated, and ventilated alveoli without blood flow (as in pulmonary embolism) are wasted breath. The lungs partly correct this by constricting vessels in poorly ventilated regions.
Thickening of the membrane (fibrosis) or fluid in the alveoli (pulmonary oedema) slows diffusion, and oxygen, with its lower solubility, is affected first.

Two physical laws govern the exchange. Dalton's law states that each gas in a mixture exerts its own partial pressure independently of the others, and Henry's law that the amount of a gas dissolving in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure; gas therefore always moves down its pressure gradient, from alveolar air into capillary blood for oxygen and in the opposite direction for carbon dioxide. Once in the blood, oxygen is bound to haemoglobin inside red cells, while most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate: it accumulates inside the red cell and then leaves for the plasma in exchange for chloride ions, with a smaller share carried bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin. Binding and release of both gases depend on their local partial pressures, so blood leaving the lungs holds less carbon dioxide than the tissues it will perfuse. In the fetus the same principles operate across the placenta, where the mother's blood plays the part of alveolar air.

The lungs tune ventilation and perfusion to each other locally. Ventilation is regulated by the diameter of the airways and perfusion by the diameter of the blood vessels; a rise in carbon dioxide in the alveoli, or a fall in oxygen in the blood supplying them, widens the bronchioles so that carbon dioxide can be cleared faster, complementing the constriction of vessels in poorly ventilated regions. Surfactant, secreted into the alveoli, lowers the effort needed to inflate the lungs and keeps the alveoli from collapsing on exhalation; without it the exchange surface shrinks, as in the premature newborn.

Gas exchange is assessed from the blood it produces. Pulse oximetry uses a probe on the fingertip or ear to estimate, without a blood sample, the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, but it says nothing about carbon dioxide or acid-base balance. An arterial blood gas sample, usually taken in hospital, measures the oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolved in arterial blood together with its pH, and is the test used when the question is whether exchange is failing, for example in severe pneumonia or an exacerbation of COPD, where carbon dioxide retention changes management. Lung function tests, chest X-ray and CT then separate problems of ventilation, of the membrane and of blood flow.

oxygen-transport.name: Oxygen transport
oxygen-transport.summary: Almost all oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin in red cells; how tightly it binds changes with the tissue's needs.
body: Each haemoglobin molecule carries four oxygen molecules, and a litre of arterial blood holds about 200 ml of oxygen, over 98% of it bound. The binding curve is S-shaped: haemoglobin loads fully in the lungs yet releases oxygen readily where partial pressure is low. Acid, heat and carbon dioxide, all produced by working tissue, shift the curve to release more (the Bohr effect).

Pulse oximeters estimate the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen; 95 to 100% is normal at sea level. Anaemia lowers the amount of haemoglobin, so total oxygen delivery falls even when saturation reads normal, which is why a saturation reading alone can mislead.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 240 times more tightly than oxygen, and standard oximeters cannot tell the difference.

The exchange itself happens across the alveolar wall, which is extraordinarily thin and wrapped in pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the air sacs into the blood, where red cells bind it to haemoglobin, a metalloprotein whose iron-containing haem groups each hold one oxygen molecule; carbon dioxide travels the opposite way to be exhaled. Only a small fraction of oxygen, about 1.5%, is carried dissolved in the plasma. Binding is cooperative: once the first oxygen molecule attaches, haemoglobin changes shape so that the second binds more readily, and so on, which produces the S-shaped curve and lets haemoglobin become almost fully saturated in the lungs yet give up a large share of its load in the tissues.

Pulse oximetry is the routine way of following this. A small clip-like sensor on a fingertip (or an infant's foot) shines red and infrared light through the tissue and calculates, from the difference in absorption by oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, the percentage of haemoglobin that is carrying oxygen; it also displays the pulse rate. The test is painless and non-invasive and is used in clinics, hospitals and at home for conditions that affect lung function such as COPD, asthma, heart failure, lung cancer and COVID-19, for sleep apnoea, and before, during and after surgery. In a healthy person with normal haemoglobin the reading sits in the high nineties.

Oximetry has limits that matter in illness. It reports saturation, not content: a person with severe anaemia may show a normal percentage while delivering far too little oxygen, and carbon monoxide poisoning reads falsely reassuring because the device cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin. Poor peripheral circulation, cold hands and movement degrade the signal. When precision matters, an arterial blood gas measures the dissolved oxygen directly.

co2-removal.name: Carbon dioxide removal and acid-base balance
co2-removal.summary: Carbon dioxide, the waste of metabolism, is carried mostly as bicarbonate and breathed out; the balance between the two sets blood acidity.
body: Tissues make about 200 ml of carbon dioxide a minute at rest. In the blood most of it reacts with water inside red cells to form bicarbonate and hydrogen ions; some binds to haemoglobin and a little dissolves. In the lungs the reaction reverses and the gas is exhaled.

Because carbon dioxide is an acid in solution, breathing controls blood pH within minutes: breathing faster lowers carbon dioxide and raises pH (respiratory alkalosis, as in panic-driven hyperventilation), breathing less does the opposite. The kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days, giving a second, slower control.

Normal arterial pH is tightly held at 7.35 to 7.45. Diseases that trap air (COPD), drugs that suppress breathing (opioids) or metabolic crises (diabetic ketoacidosis) disturb this balance and are diagnosed with an arterial blood gas.

Carbon dioxide travels in three forms. The largest share is converted inside red cells, where the enzyme carbonic anhydrase combines it with water to form carbonic acid, which splits at once into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions; the bicarbonate is exported to the plasma in exchange for chloride (the chloride shift) and the hydrogen ions are soaked up by haemoglobin. A smaller share binds directly to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin, and a little simply dissolves. In the lungs every step reverses: bicarbonate re-enters the red cell, carbonic anhydrase regenerates carbon dioxide and water, and the gas diffuses across the respiratory membrane into the alveolar air.

Three defences hold the pH. Chemical buffers act within seconds: in plasma the bicarbonate-carbonic acid pair, phosphate and the plasma proteins, and inside cells mainly proteins, with bicarbonate the chief buffer of the fluid around the tissues. The lungs act within minutes, raising pH by exhaling carbon dioxide; this is fast but has limited capacity against a large acid load, and it compensates for acidosis more readily than for alkalosis. The kidneys act over hours to days but can rid the body of either acid or base: tubular cells secrete hydrogen ions into the forming urine, where they are buffered by bicarbonate, dihydrogen phosphate or ammonia, and bicarbonate itself is conserved rather than excreted so that it can keep buffering the blood.

An arterial blood gas is the test that reads this system. Blood is drawn through a needle from an artery, usually at the wrist, and firm pressure is applied afterwards because arteries bleed readily. The analyser reports the pH, the partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide and a calculated bicarbonate: the oxygen level shows how well the lungs are taking oxygen in, the carbon dioxide level how well they are clearing it, and the acid-base values also reflect how the kidneys are coping. Abnormal results point to breathing problems or to disorders of metabolism, and the test is used to evaluate lung disease and to check whether oxygen therapy is working. During heavy exercise the muscles' extra carbon dioxide is matched by extra ventilation, so pH barely moves; in COPD, opioid overdose or neuromuscular weakness it accumulates and pH falls, while in diabetic ketoacidosis or kidney failure acid builds up from metabolism and the person breathes deeply and fast to blow carbon dioxide off.

lung-volumes.name: Lung volumes and capacities
lung-volumes.summary: The amounts of air the lungs move and hold, measured by spirometry and used to separate obstructive from restrictive disease.
body: A quiet breath moves about half a litre (tidal volume). Above it lies the inspiratory reserve and below it the expiratory reserve; together with tidal volume these make the vital capacity, roughly 4 to 5 litres in an adult man. Even after the deepest expiration about 1.2 litres remains as residual volume, keeping the alveoli open.

Spirometry records the forced vital capacity (FVC) and the volume blown out in the first second (FEV1). Obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) narrows the airways so FEV1 falls out of proportion to FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio drops below about 0.7. Restrictive disease (fibrosis, chest wall problems) shrinks all volumes but keeps the ratio normal.
Volumes fall with age, height and smoking and rise with training; reference values are matched to age, sex, height and ethnicity.

The volumes are defined by what a breath can add or remove. Tidal volume is the air that enters during quiet breathing; the inspiratory reserve volume is the extra that a deep breath can draw in beyond it, and the expiratory reserve volume the extra that can be forced out after a normal exhalation. Residual volume, the air left after the strongest possible expiration, cannot be measured by blowing into a spirometer at all, yet it is protective: it keeps the alveoli from collapsing between breaths so that the next inspiration does not have to reopen them. Capacities are sums of volumes. Inspiratory capacity is tidal plus inspiratory reserve, functional residual capacity is expiratory reserve plus residual, vital capacity is everything except the residual, and total lung capacity is the whole, larger in men than in women and in tall people than in short.

Spirometry is the standard measurement. Before the test the clinician checks that it is safe, since it is not performed during a chest infection, with certain heart problems or uncontrolled high blood pressure, or soon after a heart attack, stroke or some operations; height and weight are measured because the predicted values depend on them, and the person is told whether to pause inhalers. During the test they sit beside the spirometer wearing a soft nose clip, breathe in fully, seal their lips around the mouthpiece and blow out as hard and fast as they can, repeating the manoeuvre several times until the results are consistent. The test is painless and is stopped if chest pain or dizziness occurs. A reversibility test repeats the measurement after an inhaled bronchodilator to see whether the airways open, which supports a diagnosis of asthma.

Results are compared with the values expected for the person's age, sex and height and are usually reported later rather than on the day. Effort matters: a half-hearted blow mimics restriction, which is why technicians coach and repeat. Narrowed airways in asthma or COPD slow the first second of expiration, while stiff lungs or a weak chest wall shrink the volumes without slowing the flow; when spirometry is equivocal, full lung function testing that measures residual volume and gas transfer, or a bronchial challenge test, is used.

neurons.name: Neurons
neurons.summary: The nerve cell: a body with branching dendrites that receive signals and a single axon that carries them onward, sometimes for a metre.
body: The brain holds about 86 billion neurons, each connected to thousands of others through synapses. Dendrites collect incoming signals; if their sum crosses a threshold at the axon hillock, the neuron fires an all-or-nothing action potential down its axon. Axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulation that lets the impulse jump between gaps and travel up to 120 metres per second.

Neurons communicate chemically: an arriving impulse releases a neurotransmitter such as glutamate, GABA, dopamine or acetylcholine into the synaptic gap, and the receiving cell is excited or inhibited depending on its receptors. Most drugs acting on the nervous system change this step.
Glial cells outnumber neurons and feed, insulate and protect them. Unlike most cells, adult neurons rarely divide, which is why injury to the brain and spinal cord is so hard to repair.

At rest the inside of a neuron is negative relative to the outside. A stimulus that depolarises the membrane to a threshold voltage opens voltage-gated sodium channels and the action potential follows; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger spike, so information is coded in the frequency of firing rather than its size. Potassium leaving the cell then restores the resting voltage, with a brief overshoot of hyperpolarisation, and during the absolute refractory period that follows the sodium channels are inactivated and no new impulse can be generated, which limits the firing rate and keeps impulses travelling in one direction.

Conduction speed depends on insulation and calibre. In unmyelinated axons the impulse spreads continuously along the membrane, whereas in myelinated axons the voltage-gated channels are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, short unmyelinated gaps where the impulse is regenerated, so it appears to jump from node to node (saltatory conduction). Wider axons also conduct faster because ions meet less resistance. In demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, current leaks from axon segments that were previously insulated and conduction slows, which is one reason symptoms fluctuate and spread.

Neurons are supported by glia: astrocytes and oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord supply nutrients, insulate axons and shape the chemical environment around synapses. As a person learns, neurons form new circuits that act as information highways between brain regions. Disease often targets particular populations: in Parkinson's disease the dopamine-producing neurons of the basal ganglia die, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders involve too much or too little transmission at the synapse. Researchers have identified new neurons forming in the adult human brain, but how much this contributes to repair and function remains an open question.

nerve-signals.name: Nerve signals
nerve-signals.summary: Information travels as brief electrical pulses, action potentials, whose rate carries the message; at synapses it becomes chemical.
body: An action potential is a wave of sodium ions rushing into the axon followed by potassium flowing out, restoring the resting state within a millisecond. Because each pulse is identical, a stronger stimulus is signalled by more pulses per second, not bigger ones.

Sensory signals travel from receptors through the spinal cord and thalamus to the cortex; motor commands travel down the corticospinal tract, cross to the opposite side in the medulla, and leave through spinal nerves. This crossing is why a stroke in the left hemisphere weakens the right side of the body.

Local anaesthetics block sodium channels so pain signals never start; multiple sclerosis strips myelin so signals slow or fail; nerve compression, as in carpal tunnel syndrome, produces tingling and numbness along the nerve's territory.

The machinery is a set of channel and pump proteins in the membrane. The sodium-potassium pump, an ATPase, spends energy to move sodium out of the cell and potassium in, holding sodium high outside and potassium high inside; passive channels then let the ions leak back selectively, and it is the combination of pumps and channels that creates the resting potential and makes the action potential possible. Some channels are non-specific and pass any small cation, while the voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels that generate the spike open and close in a fixed sequence in response to the membrane voltage itself, which is why the impulse is all-or-nothing and travels in one direction.

A neuron has a cell body containing the nucleus, branching dendrites that receive messages and a single axon that carries them onward; axons range from less than a hair's width to the length of the spinal cord, and a fatty myelin sheath insulates them so that signals travel faster and farther. At the end of the axon the electrical signal must become chemical. The arriving impulse makes small sacs called vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; the molecules cross the gap and bind receptors on the next cell, which is either excited or suppressed depending on the receptor. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the brain, acetylcholine drives muscle contraction, and inhibitory transmitters damp activity. Synapses are not fixed: their strength changes with recent use, and this plasticity underlies learning and memory. The adult brain contains on the order of 85 billion neurons communicating across trillions of synapses.

Clinically, conduction is tested by nerve conduction studies, which stimulate a nerve electrically and time the response, and by electromyography; slowed conduction points to loss of myelin, as in Guillain-Barré syndrome, while reduced signal size points to loss of axons. Fever, low sodium or calcium and many drugs change excitability, which is why confusion, cramps or seizures can accompany metabolic illness.

reflexes.name: Reflexes
reflexes.summary: Fast, automatic responses wired through the spinal cord or brainstem that protect the body before the brain has time to decide.
body: The knee-jerk is the simplest: tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, a sensory neuron fires straight onto a motor neuron in the spinal cord, and the muscle contracts. Withdrawal from a hot object uses one more neuron and also inhibits the opposing muscles. Brainstem reflexes include the pupil's response to light, the gag and cough reflexes and the baroreceptor reflex that steadies blood pressure.

Clinicians grade tendon reflexes because they map the nervous system: a lost ankle reflex points to the S1 nerve root, brisk reflexes with a spreading pattern point to damage above the spinal cord, as after a stroke.
Reflexes can be modulated: the brain can suppress a withdrawal to keep hold of a hot cup, and spinal cord injury releases reflexes from that control, producing spasticity.

The textbook example of a withdrawal reflex is a hand touching a hot stove. Heat receptors in the skin fire, the signal enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root and excites a motor neuron in the ventral horn, and that neuron drives the biceps to flex the elbow and pull the hand away. A collateral branch of the same sensory fibre inhibits the motor neurons of the triceps so that the antagonist does not fight the movement, and in the legs a crossed extensor reflex stiffens the opposite limb so that the person does not fall when one foot is lifted from a sharp object. The stretch reflex works the other way round, resisting change: when a muscle is lengthened, its muscle spindle fires onto the motor neuron of that same muscle, which contracts, a loop that holds posture steady and is what a tap on the patellar tendon reveals. These are the simplest circuits in the somatic nervous system, needing only one sensory fibre entering the cord and one motor neuron leaving it.

Testing uses a reflex hammer swung in an arc onto the tendon while the limb is relaxed; the knee and ankle reflexes are the most often examined in the legs, with biceps, triceps and supinator in the arms. The examiner compares left with right and arms with legs, because the pattern tells more than any single response: diminished or absent reflexes suggest a problem in the peripheral nerves or roots, whereas exaggerated reflexes point to damage above the spinal motor neurons, as in stroke, spinal cord injury or compression of the cord in the neck. The assessment is qualitative, judged by eye, and depends on technique and positioning; a tense patient, an awkward posture or a thick limb can all blunt the response and mislead.

Reflex testing is therefore interpreted alongside power, tone and sensation rather than alone, and it has a wider role: the pupillary light and corneal reflexes test the brainstem in unconscious patients, and the absence of brainstem reflexes forms part of the criteria for diagnosing death by neurological criteria.

brain-functions.name: Brain functions
brain-functions.summary: Different regions specialise: the cortex for perception, movement, language and thought; deep nuclei for movement and emotion; the brainstem for life support; the cerebellum for coordination.
body: The frontal lobe plans, decides and, through the precentral gyrus, commands movement; Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus produces speech. The parietal lobe handles touch and space, the temporal lobe hearing, memory and language comprehension (Wernicke's area), and the occipital lobe vision. The insula senses the body's internal state.

Beneath the cortex, the basal ganglia select and smooth movements, the thalamus relays almost every signal to the cortex, the hypothalamus runs hormones, temperature, hunger and sleep, and the hippocampus lays down new memories. The brainstem keeps breathing and the heart going and houses the cranial nerve nuclei; the cerebellum times and coordinates movement.

Because functions are localised, the pattern of a deficit locates a lesion: right-sided weakness with lost speech points to the left middle cerebral artery territory, unsteadiness to the cerebellum, and memory loss with preserved alertness to the medial temporal lobes.

Anatomists divide the adult brain into four regions, cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum, and the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain of development map onto them. The basal nuclei beneath the cortex do not command movement directly: they compare what the cortex is planning with the general state of activity in the nervous system and so influence whether a movement is likely to happen, which is why their degeneration produces the slowness of Parkinson's disease rather than paralysis. The nearby basal forebrain modulates cortical activity in attention and memory. Within the brainstem, the midbrain controls some reflexes and is part of the circuit for eye movements, while the pons and medulla hold the centres that regulate the cardiovascular and respiratory systems and the nuclei of the cranial nerves serving the head and neck. The cerebellum, about a tenth of the brain's mass and connected to the brainstem mainly through the pons, initiates and times movements using information about balance and body position; it is engaged whenever a learned skill such as playing the piano or hitting a tennis ball is performed, and it builds the automatic programmes that let complex movements run without conscious thought.

The lobes carry out higher functions in a distributed way. The frontal lobes do much of the work of planning a schedule, imagining the future and reasoning; the parietal lobes, beyond touch and space, support reading and arithmetic; the occipital lobes process images from the eyes and link them with images stored in memory; and the temporal lobes form and retrieve memories, including those tied to music. Long-term episodic memory depends on the hippocampus and the surrounding medial temporal structures, whereas short-term working memory is localised to the prefrontal cortex.

The neurological examination is built around this map: its major sections correspond to the major regions of the central nervous system. The mental status examination tests the cerebrum in four groups, orientation and memory, language and speech, sensorium, and judgement and abstract reasoning, with bedside tasks such as recalling three words after a delay or reciting the months backwards. Losses of language (aphasias) point to Broca's or Wernicke's areas in the left hemisphere; difficulty recognising objects by touch or figures traced on the skin points to the parietal cortex; impaired planning and judgement point to the prefrontal cortex. The coordination examination, including gait, tests the cerebellum, and the cranial nerve examination the brainstem. Imaging with CT or MRI then confirms the location and nature of a lesion the examination has predicted.

sensory-systems.name: Sensory systems
sensory-systems.summary: Receptors convert light, sound, chemicals, pressure and temperature into nerve signals that the thalamus and cortex turn into perception.
body: The eye focuses light onto the retina, where rods handle dim light and cones colour; signals cross partly at the optic chiasm so each visual cortex sees the opposite half of the world. The ear turns vibration into fluid waves in the cochlea, where hair cells fire in proportion to pitch; the neighbouring semicircular canals and otolith organs sense rotation and gravity for balance.

Smell receptors in the roof of the nose project directly to the olfactory cortex and limbic system, which is why odours evoke memory so strongly; taste buds detect sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami. Skin carries receptors for touch, vibration, temperature and pain, with the fingertips and lips most densely supplied and therefore over-represented in the sensory cortex.
Pain is a protective signal, not a measurement of damage: it is amplified by inflammation and modulated by the brain, which explains phantom limb pain and the relief of distraction.

Sensation and perception are different steps. Sensation is the activation of a receptor by a stimulus; perception is the central processing that turns the resulting signals into a meaningful pattern. Receptors are classified by structure (free nerve endings, encapsulated endings or specialised receptor cells), by position relative to the stimulus (interoceptors for the body's interior, exteroceptors for the outside world, proprioceptors for position) and by the kind of energy they transduce. Transduction begins when the stimulus changes the membrane potential of the receptor: chemoreceptors for taste and smell are transmembrane proteins that bind a ligand, a molecule in food for instance, while mechanoreceptors open ion channels when they are physically deformed. Receptors also adapt, so a constant stimulus such as clothing on skin stops being perceived, whereas a change is signalled immediately.

Hearing illustrates transduction in detail. Sound funnelled down the ear canal vibrates the eardrum, the malleus, incus and stapes amplify the vibration and pass it to the fluid of the cochlea, and a travelling wave along the basilar membrane bends the stereocilia on the hair cells against an overlying membrane; this opens channels at their tips, ions rush in and an electrical signal passes to the auditory nerve. Hair cells near the wide base of the cochlea respond to high pitches and those toward the centre to low ones. Inner hair cells relay the signal while the more numerous outer hair cells amplify quiet sounds, and because human hair cells cannot regenerate, damage from loud noise, disease, injury or ageing causes permanent hearing loss.

In the central nervous system, somatosensory input enters through the spinal cord and most other senses through the brainstem, and all except smell relay in the thalamus before reaching the cortex. Fine touch and position travel up the dorsal columns, cross in the medulla and ascend in the medial lemniscus; pain and temperature cross within the spinal cord itself in the spinothalamic tract. Both reach the postcentral gyrus, where conscious perception of touch occurs. Vision is organised by visual field rather than by eye, with axons from the nasal retina crossing at the optic chiasm, and sound is localised partly from the microseconds by which it reaches one ear before the other. Because these pathways cross at predictable levels, the side and type of a sensory loss tell the clinician where a lesion lies, and the sensory examination tests touch, pain, vibration and position sense in turn.

digestion.name: Digestion
digestion.summary: Food is broken down mechanically by chewing and churning and chemically by enzymes, from starch in the mouth to proteins and fats in the small intestine.
body: Chewing mixes food with saliva, whose amylase starts on starch. The stomach adds hydrochloric acid, which unfolds proteins and kills microbes, and pepsin, which begins their breakdown; it churns the mix into a paste called chyme and releases it into the duodenum a few millilitres at a time.

In the duodenum, bile from the liver emulsifies fat into droplets and pancreatic juice supplies the main enzymes: lipase for fat, amylase for starch and proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) for protein. Enzymes on the intestinal lining finish the job, splitting sugars and peptides into single molecules ready for absorption.

Digestion is regulated by nerves and hormones: the sight and smell of food prime the stomach (vagus nerve), gastrin drives acid, and cholecystokinin from the duodenum squeezes the gallbladder and slows the stomach when fat arrives.

The small intestine is where most chemical digestion and almost all absorption take place, and the final steps happen on the surface of the lining itself. Fixed to the membranes of the microvilli, the brush border enzymes finish what the pancreas started: sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose, maltase converts maltose to glucose, and aminopeptidase and dipeptidase clip peptides down to single amino acids. The brush border also controls the pancreas's most dangerous products: enteropeptidase converts inactive trypsinogen to trypsin only once it reaches the intestine, and trypsin then activates the other pancreatic proteases, so the pancreas does not digest itself. Fat is handled differently: lingual and gastric lipases make a start in the mouth and stomach, but most triglyceride arrives in the duodenum undigested and depends on bile to emulsify it before pancreatic lipase can act.

Control is shared between the nervous and endocrine systems. Nerves link the brain and spinal cord to the gut, so the brain can signal the salivary glands as soon as food is seen or smelled, and both arms of the autonomic nervous system influence the process, the parasympathetic nerves stimulating secretion and peristalsis and the sympathetic nerves tending to inhibit them. The lining of the stomach and small intestine also releases its own hormones, among them gastrin, secretin and cholecystokinin, and specialised enteroendocrine cells in the small intestine convert the detection of nutrients into hormone signals, including the incretins GLP-1 and GIP, that reach the brain and the pancreas. Signals also travel from gut to brain through the vagal and spinal nerves within fractions of a second, far faster than hormones diffusing through the blood.

When the sequence is disturbed, symptoms follow the mechanism. After stomach surgery, food can move too quickly from the stomach into the duodenum, the gut releases more hormones than normal and the result is dumping syndrome, with cramps, faintness and diarrhoea after meals. Because digestion depends on nerves, hormones, gut bacteria, blood supply and the organs acting together, clinicians assess it by asking what fails: upper endoscopy to inspect the lining, tests of pancreatic enzyme output when fat is poorly digested, and breath or blood tests when a single brush border enzyme such as lactase is suspected to be deficient.

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.summary: Nutrients cross the lining of the small intestine into blood and lymph; the colon reclaims water and salts.
body: The small intestine's folds, finger-like villi and microscopic microvilli multiply its surface area to around 30 square metres. Sugars and amino acids are pumped into the cells and pass into capillaries that drain to the portal vein and the liver. Fats are rebuilt inside the cells into chylomicrons and enter the lymphatic lacteals, bypassing the liver at first.

Iron and calcium are absorbed mainly in the duodenum, most other nutrients in the jejunum, and vitamin B12 and bile salts only in the terminal ileum, which is why disease or surgery there causes specific deficiencies.

About nine litres of fluid enter the gut daily (drink plus secretions); the small intestine absorbs most and the colon nearly all the rest, leaving about 100 ml in stool. Diarrhoea is a failure of this reclamation.

Absorption depends on chemical digestion having gone first. Enzymes split large molecules by hydrolysis into subunits small enough to cross the lining: pancreatic proteases, amylases and lipases break down proteins, starches and fats respectively, and enzymes anchored in the brush border of the intestinal cells finish the job, lactase for example splitting lactose into glucose and galactose. Bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets so that lipase has a far larger surface to work on. Most nutrients then cross the apical surface of the enterocyte through specific transport proteins; lipids, the fat-soluble vitamins and most water-soluble vitamins are the exceptions and use other routes. The folds, villi and microvilli give the small intestine an absorbing surface roughly six hundred times its outer surface, and a large complex meal takes about nine hours to pass through it.

The stomach absorbs very little apart from some drugs such as alcohol and aspirin, and the large intestine secretes mucus but no digestive enzymes, so whatever chemical breakdown happens there is the work of colonic bacteria. Nerves, hormones, bacteria and the blood supply all coordinate the process: hormones released from the gut lining pace the delivery of enzymes and bile, and the rich capillary and lymphatic networks beneath the epithelium carry the products away.

Clinically, absorption is judged indirectly. Weight loss, pale bulky stools, anaemia and specific deficiencies point to malabsorption, and the pattern of deficiency indicates the site: iron and folate problems suggest the upper small bowel, vitamin B12 the terminal ileum. Coeliac disease flattens the villi, pancreatic insufficiency removes the enzymes, and resection or Crohn's disease of the ileum removes the only site for B12 and bile salt uptake. Blood tests for the nutrients concerned, faecal fat or elastase measurements and endoscopic biopsy of the duodenum are the usual investigations.

gut-motility.name: Gut motility
gut-motility.summary: Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis) move contents along the tract, run by the gut's own nervous system and tuned by the vagus nerve and hormones.
body: Swallowing is voluntary at the start, then reflex: the oesophagus carries a bolus to the stomach in about ten seconds, and the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let it through and then closes to keep acid out. The stomach mixes with slow waves three times a minute; the small intestine segments to mix and propels to move; between meals a housekeeping wave sweeps residue toward the colon every 90 minutes or so.

The colon moves contents slowly, with a few strong mass movements a day, often after meals, that push stool into the rectum and trigger the urge to defecate. The internal anal sphincter relaxes automatically; the external sphincter and puborectalis are under voluntary control.
Motility disorders cause reflux, gastroparesis, constipation or irritable bowel symptoms; a mechanical block (obstruction) produces cramping pain, vomiting and absence of gas.

Two patterns of movement serve different purposes. Peristalsis propels: in the stomach the mixing waves begin gently near the top and grow stronger as they travel toward the pylorus, softening food and blending it with gastric juice into chyme. Segmentation mixes without propelling: rings of smooth muscle in the small intestine alternately contract and relax, moving contents back and forth, blending chyme with digestive juices and pressing it against the mucosa for absorption; it is most rapid in the duodenum and slower in the ileum. Between meals the small intestine switches to migrating motility complexes, the housekeeping waves that clear residue. Slowing transit is deliberate: segmentation and a reduced rate of peristalsis buy time for digestion and absorption, and sympathetic stimulation, as in anxiety, slows digestive activity further, while parasympathetic (vagal) activity speeds secretion and peristalsis.

Gastroparesis is the clearest motility disorder: movement of food from the stomach into the small intestine slows or stops although nothing is physically blocking it. Diabetes is the most common known cause, with surgery another, but in most people no cause is identified. Those affected feel full soon after starting a meal and long after finishing it, with nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, upper abdominal pain, heartburn and a poor appetite; weight loss without trying signals malnutrition, and in diabetes erratic stomach emptying makes blood glucose swing unpredictably.

Motility is assessed by measuring how fast contents move. Clinicians combine the history, examination and symptoms with tests of stomach emptying, usually a scintigraphy study in which a labelled meal is tracked through the stomach, and a diagnosis of gastroparesis requires both delayed emptying and moderate to severe symptoms, because many of the symptoms are non-specific and can be mistaken for indigestion. Upper endoscopy is used first to exclude an obstruction, and wireless motility capsules are used in research to time transit through the whole gut. Guidance advises seeking care for vomiting lasting more than an hour or signs of dehydration or malnutrition.

liver-functions.name: Liver functions
liver-functions.summary: The liver processes everything absorbed from the gut, stores and releases fuel, makes most blood proteins, detoxifies drugs and produces bile.
body: Portal blood arrives loaded with nutrients and anything else absorbed. Liver cells store glucose as glycogen and release it between meals, make new glucose from amino acids when needed, build and break down fats and cholesterol, and manufacture albumin and the clotting factors. Ammonia from protein breakdown is converted to urea for the kidneys to excrete.

Enzyme systems (the cytochrome P450 family) transform drugs, alcohol and toxins into water-soluble forms for excretion; this is why liver disease changes drug doses and why paracetamol overdose is so dangerous. Old red cells are broken down and their haem becomes bilirubin, which the liver conjugates and excretes in bile; when this fails, bilirubin accumulates and the skin turns yellow (jaundice).
Bile, about half a litre a day, is stored in the gallbladder and released to emulsify dietary fat. The liver can regenerate after losing more than half its mass.

Structurally the liver is a filter placed in series with the gut. Nutrient-rich venous blood from the small intestine drains into the hepatic portal vein, which enters the liver at the porta hepatis alongside the hepatic artery; both empty into the hepatic sinusoids, leaky capillaries running between rows of hepatocytes, so that every absorbed molecule passes a liver cell before reaching the general circulation. Hepatocytes make up most of the organ's volume, and the bile they secrete is collected in tiny canaliculi between them before flowing out through the bile ducts to the duodenum, with the gallbladder storing and concentrating it between meals.

The liver switches role with each meal. In the absorptive state, insulin drives glucose into storage as glycogen in liver and muscle and converts the excess to fat; in the post-absorptive state, as blood glucose falls, glucagon from the alpha cells of the pancreas makes the liver break glycogen back down to glucose (glycogenolysis) and, if fasting continues until glycogen is exhausted, to make new glucose and fuel from fatty acids and amino acids. This buffering is why prolonged exercise or a missed meal does not cause hypoglycaemia in a healthy person, and why liver failure and some glycogen storage disorders do.

Liver function is assessed by blood tests that read these jobs. Bilirubin, the yellow pigment from red cell breakdown, rises when the liver cannot process it or the bile ducts are blocked, and produces jaundice; a raised unconjugated fraction points to haemolysis or impaired conjugation, as in the harmless Gilbert's syndrome, whereas a raised conjugated fraction suggests liver cell disease or biliary obstruction. Albumin falls when the liver's protein synthesis is significantly impaired, but it is an unreliable gauge of severity because sepsis, inflammation, kidney protein loss, malabsorption and malnutrition lower it too. Clotting tests (prothrombin time or INR) lengthen when fewer clotting proteins are made or vitamin K is lacking, which is why clotting is checked before invasive procedures such as liver biopsy. The enzymes ALT and AST signal liver cell injury while ALP and GGT point to bile flow, and a low platelet count is a common sign of advanced chronic disease. An abnormal result is not a diagnosis: it is interpreted against previous results, history and current illness, since conditions outside the liver also change these values.

pancreatic-functions.name: Pancreatic functions
pancreatic-functions.summary: One organ, two jobs: exocrine cells pour digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum; the islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
body: About 1.5 litres of alkaline pancreatic juice a day neutralises stomach acid and delivers lipase, amylase and the protein-digesting enzymes, which are secreted as inactive precursors and switched on only in the gut so the pancreas does not digest itself. When that safeguard fails, the result is pancreatitis.

The islets sense blood glucose directly. After a meal beta cells release insulin, which tells muscle, fat and liver to take up and store glucose; between meals alpha cells release glucagon, which makes the liver release it again. This pair holds blood glucose within a narrow band around 4 to 7 mmol/L.
Type 1 diabetes destroys the beta cells; type 2 diabetes is mainly resistance to insulin's signal with a gradual failure of the beta cells to compensate.

The islets contain several cell types, not just two. Beta cells make up about three quarters of each islet and release insulin when blood glucose is high; alpha cells make up about a fifth and release glucagon when it is low; the few delta cells secrete somatostatin, and others pancreatic polypeptide. Insulin enhances glucose uptake and use by its target cells and promotes storage of the excess, notably as glycogen in the liver, which lowers blood glucose; glucagon stimulates the breakdown of that glycogen, raising it again. Because the two hormones oppose each other, the islets act as a self-correcting controller that needs no input from the brain, although autonomic nerves and gut hormones released after a meal modulate the response.

The exocrine tissue is the bulk of the organ. Its two main roles, in the NIDDK's summary, are making insulin and making the digestive juices that break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the intestine. Pancreatitis is inflammation that occurs when those enzymes damage the pancreas itself: acute pancreatitis comes on suddenly, with gallstones a common cause, and usually settles, whereas chronic pancreatitis does not heal or improve and gradually destroys both enzyme-producing and hormone-producing tissue, so that food is malabsorbed and diabetes can follow.

Pancreatic function is assessed from both sides. Blood glucose and glycated haemoglobin reflect the endocrine side, and diabetes mellitus is diagnosed when insulin production fails or target cells stop responding to it. Serum amylase and lipase rise sharply in acute pancreatitis, while faecal elastase and the presence of fat in the stool indicate exocrine insufficiency. Imaging with ultrasound, CT or MRCP shows inflammation, gallstones, cysts and ductal change.

filtration.name: Glomerular filtration
filtration.summary: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the nephron, about 180 litres a day, while cells and proteins stay behind.
body: Each kidney holds about a million nephrons. In the glomerulus a tuft of leaky capillaries sits inside Bowman's capsule; the pressure difference drives an ultrafiltrate of plasma through a three-layer sieve that blocks cells and almost all protein. The glomerular filtration rate (GFR), roughly 120 ml per minute in a healthy young adult, is the standard measure of kidney function.

The kidney keeps GFR steady across a wide range of blood pressures by adjusting its afferent and efferent arterioles; drugs that act on these vessels (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors) can drop filtration in a dehydrated patient.
Because creatinine is filtered freely and barely reabsorbed, its blood level rises as GFR falls, which is how kidney disease is staged. Protein in the urine means the sieve is damaged.

The sieve has three layers: the fenestrated endothelium of the glomerular capillary, the glomerular basement membrane and the podocytes whose interlocking foot processes form the final barrier, with the filtrate collecting in Bowman's space beyond. Filtration is by size and charge, so water, ions, glucose, urea and small peptides pass while cells and all but the smallest proteins are held back. The driving force is a balance of Starling forces: the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillary pushes fluid out and is opposed by the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins and by the pressure already in the capsule; the net filtration pressure is the modest difference. Because the glomerulus sits between two arterioles, the kidney can set that pressure by adjusting their resistances, and two built-in mechanisms, the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback from the macula densa, hold renal blood flow and filtration steady across a wide range of arterial pressures.

Nearly all of the filtrate is reabsorbed, so a huge filtration rate produces only a litre or two of urine. The rate is slightly higher in men than in women and declines slowly with age. It can be measured directly from the clearance of a marker that is freely filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed by the tubules, but in routine practice it is estimated from the serum creatinine, adjusted for age and sex, as the eGFR, and this estimate is what stages chronic kidney disease.

The estimate has a well-known blind spot. When some nephrons are lost, the survivors filter harder, so the overall rate falls far less than the amount of damaged tissue would suggest and symptoms appear only when very little function remains. Dehydration, heart failure and drugs that relax the efferent arteriole or constrict the afferent one can all drop filtration abruptly, which is why kidney function is checked when these treatments are started, while protein or blood in the urine signals that the barrier itself is damaged, as in glomerulonephritis or diabetic kidney disease.

reabsorption.name: Tubular reabsorption and secretion
reabsorption.summary: The tubules reclaim over 99% of the filtered water and salt and all the glucose, and add wastes and excess ions to what remains.
body: The proximal tubule recovers about two thirds of the filtered water and sodium and all the glucose and amino acids; when blood glucose is high, as in uncontrolled diabetes, the transporters are overwhelmed and glucose spills into the urine. The loop of Henle builds a salt gradient in the medulla that allows water to be drawn out later. The distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune sodium, potassium and acid under hormonal control.

Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption (and potassium loss); antidiuretic hormone opens water channels in the collecting duct to concentrate urine. Diuretic drugs block specific transporters: loop diuretics in the thick ascending limb, thiazides in the distal tubule.
Secretion works the other way: the tubules actively pump potassium, hydrogen ions, drugs and organic acids into the urine, which is how penicillin and many other drugs are cleared.

Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, and the division of labour within each is simple: the glomerulus filters the blood and the tubule returns what the body needs while leaving wastes behind. The final adjustment is made in the collecting ducts, which under the influence of ADH can recover almost all of the water passing through them during dehydration or almost none during over-hydration. ADH does this by stimulating the insertion of aquaporin water channels (and urea transporters) into the cell membranes; when ADH falls the aquaporins are withdrawn and water stays in the urine. Aldosterone acts on the same segments to recover sodium, and because sodium reabsorption is coupled to potassium secretion, a high aldosterone level causes potassium loss. Renin acts indirectly: when blood pressure falls, sympathetic nerves stimulate its release, angiotensin II is generated and aldosterone production rises, so more sodium and water are retained and blood volume is restored.

The kidney also protects reabsorption by holding filtration steady. Two internal mechanisms, the myogenic response of the arterioles and tubuloglomerular feedback, keep the glomerular filtration rate roughly constant across a range of blood pressures without any outside instruction: when the macula densa cells of the distal tubule sense a change in the filtrate flowing past them, they release ATP and adenosine, which constrict the afferent arteriole and reduce filtration. This autoregulation is why kidney function survives everyday swings in blood pressure during exercise and sleep, and why it can fail abruptly in shock or severe dehydration, when pressure drops below the range the kidney can compensate for.

Reabsorption cannot be measured directly in a patient, so it is assessed by what reaches the urine and what remains in the blood. Glucose in the urine signals that blood glucose has exceeded the tubule's transport capacity, as in diabetes mellitus, though it is no longer used to diagnose diabetes. A standard kidney work-up pairs a urinalysis and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio with blood creatinine (from which the estimated glomerular filtration rate is calculated), urea and electrolytes, so disordered sodium, potassium or water handling shows up as abnormal blood electrolytes alongside an inappropriately concentrated or dilute urine.

urine-formation.name: Urine formation and excretion
urine-formation.summary: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion leave one to two litres of urine a day, carried by the ureters to the bladder and released under voluntary control.
body: Urine is mostly water carrying urea, creatinine, uric acid, salts and any drug metabolites the body needs to lose. Its colour reflects concentration; its composition, read by a dipstick, reveals infection (leucocytes, nitrites), blood, protein, glucose or ketones.

Peristalsis in the ureters delivers urine to the bladder, which stretches to hold 400 to 600 ml. Stretch receptors signal fullness at around 200 ml; the micturition reflex contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter, while the external sphincter is released voluntarily. Children learn this control between two and four years; strokes, spinal injury and prostate enlargement disturb it.
Kidney stones form when salts crystallise in concentrated urine; keeping urine dilute is the simplest prevention.

The first step is filtration in the glomeruli, which together form filtrate at a rate called the glomerular filtration rate; of the enormous volume filtered each day, about ninety-nine per cent is reabsorbed back into the blood along the tubules, so that only one to two litres leave as urine. Reabsorption is selective: glucose, amino acids and most of the salt and water are reclaimed, while urea, creatinine and many drugs are left behind or actively secreted into the tubule. The final composition is adjusted in the collecting ducts under the control of antidiuretic hormone, which decides how much water is kept, and aldosterone, which decides how much sodium.

Emptying is a spinal reflex with a cortical veto. Stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal through the sacral spinal cord; the resulting parasympathetic outflow contracts the detrusor muscle and relaxes the involuntary internal urethral sphincter, while at the same time the cord inhibits the somatic motor neurons so that the skeletal muscle of the external sphincter also relaxes. Conscious effort can keep the external sphincter closed and defer voiding until the volume becomes large enough to override it. The reflex runs unchecked in infants; children learn to assert external sphincter control, and the control is lost again after strokes, spinal cord injury or dementia.

The kidneys also carry out the final step in making active vitamin D, which regulates calcium, and secrete erythropoietin, which drives red cell production, so failing kidneys cause bone disease and anaemia as well as fluid overload. Kidney function is followed with blood creatinine and the estimated filtration rate derived from it, with urine dipstick and microscopy for protein, blood, cells and crystals, and with ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder, including measurement of the volume left after voiding when retention is suspected. Urinary problems range from the inconvenience of incontinence to the life-threatening loss of filtration in kidney failure.
