fluid-balance.name: Fluid balance
fluid-balance.summary: Water in equals water out: thirst, antidiuretic hormone and the kidneys keep the body's 40 litres of fluid within a litre of its set point.
body: An adult is about 60% water: two thirds inside cells, the rest in the tissue spaces and in blood plasma. Intake of about 2.5 litres a day (drink, food and metabolism) matches loss in urine, sweat, breath and stool. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense a rise in blood concentration of only 1 to 2% and trigger both thirst and antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys retain water.

Volume is sensed separately by stretch receptors in the heart and pressure receptors in the arteries; a fall activates the sympathetic system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade, which retains salt and water and constricts vessels. Heart failure and cirrhosis activate these pathways inappropriately and cause swelling (oedema).
Dehydration presents with thirst, dark urine, dizziness on standing and a rising heart rate; in infants and the elderly it can progress quickly.

The water-conserving loop runs through the posterior pituitary. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are especially sensitive to the concentration of sodium and other solutes; when osmolarity rises, during dehydration or after a very salty meal, they trigger thirst and signal the posterior pituitary to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH acts on the principal cells lining the collecting ducts, inserting aquaporin water channels into their membranes so that water leaves the filtrate osmotically and the urine becomes concentrated; when ADH falls, fewer channels are inserted and the urine is dilute. The loop is self-correcting: as osmolarity falls back, the osmoreceptors reduce ADH secretion. Angiotensin II, generated when blood volume or pressure is low, adds a second drive to the thirst centre. The system fails in diabetes insipidus, where chronic under-production of ADH leaves a person constantly thirsty yet unable to retain the water they drink, and it is suppressed by alcohol, which inhibits ADH release and increases urine output, part of the mechanism of a hangover.

Dehydration arises when intake does not keep pace with losses from diarrhoea, vomiting, heavy sweating, fever or excessive urination, the last often caused by diabetes or diuretic medicines; heat, heavy alcohol use and old age raise the risk, because some people lose their sense of thirst as they age. Adults notice thirst, dark yellow urine passed less often, dizziness or light-headedness, headache, tiredness and a dry mouth, lips and eyes. In babies the signs are a sunken fontanelle, sunken eyes, few or no tears when crying, fewer wet nappies and drowsiness or irritability. Severe dehydration is life-threatening and shows as confusion, a rapid heartbeat and breathing, shock and little or no urine.

Assessment is mostly clinical. Examination looks for low blood pressure or a fall in pressure on standing, slow capillary refill in the fingertips and skin that springs back slowly when pinched; a blood or urine test checks the balance of salts. NHS guidance advises urgent GP or NHS 111 contact for unusual tiredness, dizziness on standing that does not settle, very dark or much reduced urine or a fast heart rate or breathing, and an emergency call when skin is pale, grey or blue and cold, breathing is difficult or the person is confused or hard to wake.

electrolytes.name: Electrolytes
electrolytes.summary: Sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate carry charge, set the water distribution between compartments and make nerves and muscles excitable.
body: Sodium is the main ion outside cells and, with its water, sets blood volume; the kidneys and aldosterone keep its concentration near 140 mmol/L. Potassium is concentrated inside cells; its blood level, normally 3.5 to 5, must stay in a narrow band because both high and low values disturb the heart's rhythm.

Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D and is needed for muscle contraction, clotting and nerve signalling; low levels cause tingling and cramps, high levels stones, bone pain and confusion. Magnesium is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and follows potassium.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, kidney disease and hormone disorders are the usual causes of imbalance, detected on a basic metabolic panel.

Six ions do most of the work: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium and phosphate. Between them they set nerve and muscle excitability, control the release of hormones, govern the permeability of cell membranes, buffer the body fluids and determine where water sits between the compartments. Sodium, the dominant cation outside cells, accounts for about half of the osmotic pressure difference between the inside and outside of cells, so where sodium goes, water follows; Western diets supply far more sodium chloride than the body needs. Potassium is kept high inside cells by the sodium-potassium pump, which spends ATP to move sodium out and potassium in. The kidney is the main site of regulation: aldosterone and angiotensin II control the exchange of sodium for potassium in the collecting tubule, and the kidneys excrete most of the ions the body needs to lose, with smaller amounts leaving in sweat and faeces.

Calcium behaves differently because most of the body's store is locked in bone, which acts as a mineral reserve for the rest of the tissues. In blood a little more than half of the calcium is bound to proteins and the remainder is ionised, and it is the ionised fraction that supports muscle contraction, enzyme activity and clotting. Parathyroid hormone, calcitriol (active vitamin D) and calcitonin together regulate calcium and phosphate. Bicarbonate is the chief buffer of the extracellular fluid, and chloride helps maintain blood volume and pressure.

The electrolyte panel, a routine blood test, measures sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate; magnesium and calcium are measured separately or as part of a wider metabolic panel, and the anion gap calculated from the panel shows whether the blood is too acidic or not acidic enough. An imbalance simply means that one or more electrolytes is too high or too low, and it usually follows a change in body water, since in health the water taken in matches the water lost. Heavy sweating during prolonged exercise or heat exposure, vomiting and diarrhoea, diuretics and kidney or hormonal disease all upset the balance, and because potassium and calcium alter cardiac and neuromuscular excitability, severe derangements are treated as emergencies and monitored with an ECG.

hormones.name: Hormones
hormones.summary: Chemical messengers released into the blood that act on distant cells carrying the right receptor, coordinating growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction over minutes to years.
body: Hormones come in families. Peptides and proteins (insulin, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone) act on surface receptors and work within minutes. Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen) are made from cholesterol, pass into cells and switch genes on or off over hours. Amines include adrenaline, fast and short-lived, and thyroid hormone, slow and long-lasting.

The same hormone can do different things in different tissues: adrenaline speeds the heart, dilates airways and releases glucose all at once, which is exactly what a fight-or-flight response needs. Concentrations are tiny, measured in picomoles, so small changes matter and assays must be precise.
Because hormones reach everywhere, endocrine disease is multi-system: an overactive thyroid causes weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and anxiety together.

Chemistry determines how a hormone travels and where it acts. Amine hormones are built from a single amino acid, tryptophan or tyrosine; peptide and protein hormones are chains of amino acids; steroids are derived from cholesterol. Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble, so they diffuse through the cell membrane and bind receptors inside the cell, usually altering which genes are transcribed. Every other hormone is water-soluble and must bind a receptor on the cell surface, typically coupled to a G protein that triggers a cascade of second messengers inside the cell; this is why water-soluble hormones act quickly and lipid-soluble hormones act slowly but durably. A hormone only affects cells that carry its receptor, which is how a signal that reaches every tissue can have selective effects: aldosterone raises blood sodium while cortisol raises blood glucose.

Hormone disorders arise when a level is too high or too low, or when the body no longer responds to a hormone normally; diabetes is the most common endocrine disease in the United States. Treatment works on the same logic in reverse: controlling how much hormone a gland makes when there is excess, or replacing the hormone when there is too little.

Hormones are measured in blood, urine or saliva, and interpretation depends on timing and context. Cortisol varies through the day, so it is sampled early in the morning or collected over a full day; thyroid hormones can be measured as total (bound plus free) or as the free fraction that is biologically active, and a low free thyroxine may reflect an underactive thyroid but also severe acute illness or malnutrition. Medicines, obesity, depression and stress can all distort results, so an unexpected value is usually repeated and read together with the hormone that controls it before a diagnosis is made.

hormone-regulation.name: Hormone regulation: the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
hormone-regulation.summary: The hypothalamus tells the pituitary, the pituitary tells the glands, and the glands' hormones report back: a chain of command that links the brain to the endocrine system.
body: Releasing hormones from the hypothalamus travel down a private portal system to the anterior pituitary, which secretes the tropic hormones: thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, the gonadotropins, growth hormone and prolactin. The posterior pituitary stores two hormones made in the hypothalamus itself, antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.

Each axis is a loop: for the thyroid, TRH drives TSH, TSH drives thyroxine, and thyroxine suppresses both. So a failing thyroid produces a high TSH, while a pituitary problem produces low TSH with low thyroxine; the pair of results tells you where the fault lies.
Stress, sleep, light and season act on the hypothalamus, which is why cortisol peaks in the early morning, growth hormone surges in deep sleep and the menstrual cycle can stop under severe stress.

Anatomically the two lobes of the pituitary are different tissues. The posterior lobe is neural tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus down the infundibulum (pituitary stalk), whereas the anterior lobe is glandular tissue that develops from the roof of the primitive digestive tract. The hypophyseal portal system is a network of vessels that carries hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones straight into the anterior lobe without them entering the general circulation, so tiny quantities reach their target undiluted. Cortisol illustrates how feedback is layered: it inhibits both the hypothalamus and the pituitary, so when the hypothalamus detects a rising level of a target-gland hormone it tells the pituitary to stop releasing the corresponding tropic hormone.

Because secretion is pulsatile and follows a daily rhythm, a single random hormone level is often uninformative. Clinicians therefore sample at the right time (cortisol early in the morning, when it is expected to peak) and, when the question is whether a gland can respond, use dynamic tests that stimulate or suppress the axis and watch the response. A flat response of ACTH and cortisol to stimulation points to pituitary disease, whereas a delayed but exaggerated response suggests the fault lies in the hypothalamus; a suppression test checks that cortisol production can still be switched off. Paired measurements of the tropic hormone and the gland hormone, such as TSH with thyroxine, or ACTH with cortisol, locate the fault in the same way.

Pituitary disease is often a mass effect: a tumour can damage the normal hormone-releasing cells so the gland under-produces some or all of its hormones, and a mass is suspected when a deficiency of one axis is accompanied by deficiencies of other pituitary hormones or a raised prolactin. The axis is also vulnerable to dysregulation under sustained physical or psychological stress, and results can be distorted by medicines, obesity, depression and acute illness, so abnormal findings are usually repeated and interpreted alongside imaging of the pituitary.

feedback-mechanisms.name: Feedback mechanisms and homeostasis
feedback-mechanisms.summary: Negative feedback, where a rise in the output switches off its own production, holds temperature, glucose, blood pressure and hormones near their set points.
body: A thermostat is the model: a sensor measures the variable, a control centre compares it with a set point, and an effector corrects the error. Body temperature is held near 37 °C by the hypothalamus, which orders sweating and skin vasodilation when hot and shivering and vasoconstriction when cold; fever is a deliberate resetting of the set point by inflammatory signals.

Glucose is held by the insulin-glucagon pair, calcium by parathyroid hormone, blood pressure by baroreflexes and the kidneys, oxygen and carbon dioxide by the breathing centres. Diseases are often a broken loop: in type 1 diabetes the effector (insulin) is missing; in Cushing's disease the control centre ignores the feedback.
Positive feedback is rare and used for events that must run to completion: the surge of oxytocin in labour, blood clotting and the sodium rush of an action potential.

Every regulated variable has a set point, the value around which its normal range fluctuates, and a negative feedback loop has three components: a sensor that measures the variable, a control centre that compares the reading with the set point, and an effector that reverses the deviation. The loop's purpose is as much restraint as correction: it prevents an excessive response and winds down as the stimulus is removed. The endocrine system shows the same logic at the level of whole glands: when the hypothalamus detects a rising level of hormone from a target organ, it signals the pituitary to stop releasing the hormone that drives that organ. Positive feedback, by contrast, intensifies a change until an end point is reached; in labour, oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which stretch the cervix further and release more oxytocin, a cycle that stops only when the baby is born.

Temperature control is the textbook negative feedback system. The thermostat is the preoptic area of the hypothalamus, which receives input from peripheral receptors in the skin, reporting surface temperature, and central receptors in the viscera, spinal cord and hypothalamus itself, reporting core temperature. When heat production exceeds need, as during exercise, the hypothalamus opens the skin circulation so heat escapes and drives sweating; in the cold it does the reverse, constricting skin vessels, and if that is insufficient it triggers shivering and activates brown fat to generate heat.

Fever is not a failure of the thermostat but a change in its setting. Infection or inflammation releases cytokines, among them interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor-alpha, which drive production of prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus and shift the set point upward; the body then behaves as if it were cold, so a person feels chilled and shivers while their temperature climbs. This distinguishes fever from hyperthermia, in which core temperature rises beyond the set point and beyond the hypothalamus's ability to regulate it, as in heat stroke, which is why hyperthermia is more dangerous than fever at a similar reading and why antipyretic drugs, which act on the prostaglandin step, lower a fever but not heat stroke. Clinically, feedback loops are assessed by measuring the variable and its controlling signal together: a temperature with the clinical context, or a hormone with the tropic hormone that drives it.

endocrine-glands.name: The major endocrine glands
endocrine-glands.summary: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets, gonads and pineal each make a signature set of hormones; several other organs, including the heart, kidneys, gut and fat, make hormones too.
body: The pituitary controls growth, thyroid and adrenal function, reproduction, milk production and water balance. The thyroid sets the metabolic rate through thyroxine; the four parathyroids behind it raise blood calcium. The adrenal cortex makes cortisol (stress and glucose), aldosterone (salt and blood pressure) and androgens; its medulla makes adrenaline. The islets of the pancreas make insulin and glucagon; the testes make testosterone and the ovaries oestrogen and progesterone; the pineal makes melatonin.

Less famous sources matter clinically: the heart releases natriuretic peptides when stretched (used to diagnose heart failure), the kidneys release erythropoietin to make red cells, the gut makes incretins that boost insulin, and fat tissue makes leptin, which signals energy stores to the brain.
In this atlas the pituitary and adrenal glands are modelled; the thyroid and parathyroids are not part of the dataset.

What makes a gland endocrine is the route its product takes. Endocrine glands are ductless: they secrete hormones directly into the interstitial fluid and bloodstream, which carries them to every tissue, whereas exocrine glands such as sweat glands deliver their secretions through ducts to a surface or cavity. The pancreas is both: most of its tissue is exocrine and makes digestive enzymes, while the scattered islets act as an endocrine gland, releasing insulin when blood glucose rises and glucagon when it falls. Because it relies on chemical signalling through the circulation, the endocrine system is slower than the nervous system and suited to maintaining the internal environment, growth and reproduction rather than to split-second responses.

The glands form a hierarchy with the pea-sized pituitary at the base of the brain near the top: it releases adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which tells the two adrenal glands sitting on top of the kidneys to make cortisol, a hormone that helps regulate blood pressure, damp down inflammation and turn food into energy. The system as a whole influences growth and development, metabolism, sexual function and mood, so a disorder of one gland tends to produce symptoms across many body systems.

Endocrine disease arises when a gland makes too much or too little hormone, or when the body stops responding to a hormone normally. Thyroid disorders, whether an underactive or an overactive gland, are often autoimmune, as in Hashimoto's disease and Graves' disease, and glands can also be affected together: in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, an inherited disorder, tumours develop in the parathyroids, the pancreas and the pituitary. Assessment usually starts with blood tests that pair the gland's hormone with the pituitary hormone that controls it, followed by imaging of the gland concerned.

gender-affirming-hormones.name: Gender-affirming hormone therapy: what changes in the body
gender-affirming-hormones.summary: Feminising therapy (oestradiol with testosterone suppression) and masculinising therapy (testosterone) shift the body's sex-hormone environment towards that of the affirmed gender, producing gradual changes in fat, muscle, skin, hair, breast tissue and the reproductive organs over months to years, some of them permanent.
body: Gender-affirming hormone therapy is one of the medical options for trans women, trans men and non-binary people who experience gender incongruence, which the World Health Organization's ICD-11 classifies under conditions related to sexual health and not as a mental illness. Treatment follows the WPATH, Endocrine Society and UCSF guidelines; in England it is started by NHS gender dysphoria clinics, with prescribing and monitoring often shared with the GP. Both regimens reduce fertility, so fertility preservation (storing sperm or eggs) is discussed before starting. Whether to start, which preparation to use and for how long are individual decisions made with a specialist team, and some effects reverse if treatment stops while others, once established, are permanent.

Feminising therapy uses oestradiol, given as a patch, gel, tablet or injection, with a medicine that suppresses testosterone (spironolactone, cyproterone acetate or a GnRH analogue), which is no longer needed once the testes have been removed. Ethinylestradiol, the oestrogen used in the combined contraceptive pill, is not used for this purpose because it carries a higher clot risk and its level cannot be monitored. The guideline timetables give reduced libido and fewer spontaneous erections within one to three months; softer skin, fat moving to the hips and thighs, loss of muscle mass and the start of breast growth at three to six months, with breast development at its maximum after two to three years; and shrinking testes with falling sperm production. Breast tissue that has developed does not disappear if oestradiol is stopped. Facial and body hair becomes finer and slower growing from about six to twelve months but rarely disappears, so many trans women also use electrolysis or laser hair removal. Oestradiol does not raise the pitch of the voice or alter the adult skeleton, and the prostate remains in place.

Masculinising therapy uses testosterone, usually as a daily gel or as injections given at intervals from weekly to every few months depending on the preparation. Skin becomes oilier and acne is common early, periods usually stop within two to six months, and the clitoris enlarges while the vaginal lining thins and becomes drier. The voice deepens over the first year and the change is permanent; facial and body hair start to grow within about three to six months and keep increasing for three to five years; muscle grows and fat moves to the abdomen; male-pattern hair loss can develop. Facial and body hair growth and clitoral enlargement also persist if testosterone is stopped. Testosterone raises the red cell count and is not reliable contraception, because ovulation can still occur after periods stop. Height and bone structure do not change, and breast tissue may lose some fat but does not go away; it is removed only by chest surgery. The uterus, ovaries and cervix remain unless they are removed, so anyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people, still needs cervical screening.

Monitoring follows the guidelines: oestradiol and testosterone are measured every few months in the first year and then once or twice a year, aiming for the range typical of the affirmed gender, alongside blood pressure, lipids, glucose or HbA1c, weight and liver function. Potassium and kidney function are checked on spironolactone because it is potassium-sparing, haemoglobin and haematocrit on testosterone because a raised red cell mass (erythrocytosis) thickens the blood, and some guidelines (the Endocrine Society) also include prolactin, since oestrogen can raise it. Bone density is assessed after the gonads have been removed if hormones are not being taken. The main risk of oestrogen is venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), highest with oral preparations, smoking and immobility, so transdermal oestradiol is preferred for people at higher risk. Sudden pain or swelling in a calf, or breathlessness or chest pain, needs urgent medical assessment, whatever the preparation. Screening invitations follow the gender recorded with the GP, so some trans people need to ask for the screening that matches their anatomy: breast screening for trans women on long-term oestrogen and for trans men and non-binary people who have not had chest surgery, and cervical screening for anyone who still has a cervix. The prostate is not removed in feminising surgery, so prostate symptoms are still assessed in the usual way and a PSA result is interpreted in the light of testosterone suppression.

menopause.name: Menopause
menopause.summary: The permanent end of periods when the ovaries run out of responsive follicles and stop making oestrogen; it happens at an average age of 51 in the UK, is preceded by a perimenopause of irregular cycles and symptoms, and its effects on bone, the heart and the genitourinary tissues last long after the flushes have settled.
body: The menopause is the point at which the ovaries stop releasing eggs and making meaningful amounts of oestrogen, so periods stop for good: the follicle store is nearly spent, oestradiol and inhibin drop and FSH rises. In the UK it happens at an average age of 51, usually between 45 and 55, and is defined after 12 consecutive months without a period. The same change happens in anyone with ovaries, including trans men and non-binary people who are not taking testosterone or who stop it, although periods are often already absent on testosterone, so the transition may only become clear on hormone testing or when symptoms appear. The perimenopause, with irregular and often anovulatory cycles, lasts several years, and symptoms begin while periods continue. Fertility falls but does not vanish, so contraception is advised until periods have stopped for two years under 50 or one year over 50, and can usually stop at 55. Over 45 the diagnosis rests on the pattern of periods and symptoms; NICE advises against FSH testing except under 45.

The most characteristic symptoms are vasomotor: hot flushes and night sweats, which disturb sleep and can leave people tired and low. Mood changes, poor concentration, joint aches and lower libido are common. The vagina, vulva, urethra and bladder base thin as oestrogen falls, giving the genitourinary syndrome of menopause: dryness, pain during sex, urinary urgency and recurrent urinary infections, which persist without treatment. Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause, or unscheduled bleeding that continues beyond the first months of hormone replacement therapy, is not a menopausal symptom and is a reason to see a GP urgently: NICE advises an urgent referral for women aged 55 and over with postmenopausal bleeding, so that endometrial cancer can be excluded.

Oestrogen restrains bone-resorbing osteoclasts, so bone loss accelerates after the menopause and wrist, spine and hip fractures become more likely; weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D and, where bone density is low, medicines such as alendronate are the mainstays of prevention. The lipid profile becomes less favourable and the pelvic floor supports weaken. Premature ovarian insufficiency is menopause before 40, when hormone replacement is advised at least until the usual age. Surgical menopause, after removal of both ovaries, is often more intense because the hormones disappear overnight; the same applies to trans men and non-binary people whose ovaries are removed, in whom testosterone usually maintains bone unless it is interrupted.

Management starts with lifestyle measures. Hormone replacement therapy is the most effective treatment for flushes and night sweats and also protects bone; anyone who still has a uterus also takes a progestogen, so that unopposed oestrogen does not thicken the lining. Transdermal oestrogen is preferred where there is a risk of venous thromboembolism, and combined HRT slightly raises breast cancer risk with longer use, which falls after stopping. For most women with troublesome symptoms the benefits of HRT outweigh the risks, and the NHS advises that the risks are small when it is started around the usual age of menopause; the balance depends on age, time since the last period, the type of HRT and personal risk factors, and is reviewed regularly. Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms and recurrent urinary infections with very little absorption; cognitive behavioural therapy and some antidepressants, prescribed off-label, are non-hormonal options.

menstrual-cycle.name: The menstrual cycle
menstrual-cycle.summary: A roughly monthly cycle in which one ovary matures and releases an egg while the uterus builds a lining and then sheds it as a period if no pregnancy follows, timed throughout by hormones.
body: The menstrual cycle is the roughly monthly sequence in which one ovary matures and releases an egg while the uterus prepares a lining and then sheds it if no pregnancy occurs. Day 1 is the first day of bleeding, and the average cycle is about 28 days: the NHS counts anything from 21 to 40 days as normal as long as the pattern is regular for that person. Two cycles run in step, one in the ovary and one in the uterus, and both are driven by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis: the hypothalamus releases gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in pulses, the pituitary answers with follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH), and the ovary with oestradiol, progesterone and inhibin, which feed back on both.

In the follicular phase the FSH rise that follows the hormone fall at the end of the previous cycle recruits a group of follicles, whose granulosa cells make oestradiol; rising oestradiol and inhibin then suppress FSH, so only the most sensitive follicle survives. When oestradiol stays high for a couple of days the feedback turns positive, the pituitary releases a surge of LH and the follicle ruptures about a day later: ovulation, around day 14 of a 28-day cycle. The emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone for a fairly constant 14 days, so differences in cycle length come mostly from the follicular phase. Without fertilisation it degenerates and both hormones fall; if an embryo implants, its human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) keeps it working, so a missed period is often the first sign of pregnancy.

The uterus follows the ovary. Falling progesterone constricts the spiral arteries of the endometrium, so the functional layer becomes ischaemic and is shed as the menstrual flow, usually over about 5 days, with 3 to 8 days counted as normal; bleeding that interferes with daily life counts as heavy, whatever the measured volume. Oestradiol then regrows the lining from the basal layer through the proliferative phase and makes the cervical mucus clear and stretchy at ovulation. In the secretory phase progesterone makes the glands secrete glycogen-rich fluid ready for implantation, thickens the mucus again and raises the basal body temperature slightly. Period pain comes from prostaglandins released by the shedding lining, which make the myometrium contract.

Not every cycle is ovulatory: anovulatory cycles are common in the first year or two after the first period (menarche) and again in the perimenopause, and are often irregular and sometimes heavy, because oestradiol builds the lining with no progesterone to stabilise it. Hormonal contraception acts on the same axis: combined methods suppress the LH surge so that no follicle ovulates, and the bleed in the hormone-free interval is a withdrawal bleed rather than a true period, while progestogen-only methods thicken the cervical mucus and thin the lining, and some also stop ovulation. Testosterone taken by trans men and non-binary people usually stops periods within a few months, but it is not contraception, and bleeding that returns needs assessment.

pregnancy.name: Pregnancy and birth: how the body changes
pregnancy.summary: From fertilisation in the fallopian tube to birth about 40 weeks later, pregnancy remodels almost every maternal system, from blood volume and kidney filtration to insulin sensitivity.
body: Pregnancy begins with fertilisation in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, about a day after ovulation; implantation into the progesterone-primed secretory endometrium follows about a week later. The implanting embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone so that the lining is not shed; it is the hormone pregnancy tests detect. Nausea and vomiting are common in the first trimester and tend to ease as hCG falls, although the cause is not fully understood. By about 10 to 12 weeks the placenta has taken over the production of progesterone and oestrogens. Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last period, so birth is expected at about 40 weeks.

The placenta is both an exchange organ and an endocrine gland: maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi, so oxygen, glucose and antibodies cross to the fetus and waste passes back, without the circulations mixing. Blood volume rises by roughly 30 to 50%, plasma more than red cells, so the haemoglobin concentration falls (a physiological anaemia) as the need for iron rises, and cardiac output rises by about 30 to 50%. Progesterone relaxes vascular smooth muscle, so blood pressure falls in the first half of pregnancy and returns to its earlier level by term; a pressure that rises after 20 weeks, especially with protein in the urine, is the pattern of pre-eclampsia, so both are checked at every antenatal appointment.

Renal blood flow and filtration rise by about half, while the ureters dilate and drain more slowly, so urinary infection reaches the kidneys more easily. Placental hormones make maternal tissues less sensitive to insulin so that more glucose reaches the fetus; gestational diabetes develops when the pancreas cannot compensate, and a glucose tolerance test is offered to those with risk factors; treatment starts with changes to diet and physical activity, with metformin and then insulin added if blood glucose targets are not met. Relaxin softens ligaments, which lets the pelvis give a little in labour but produces pelvic girdle and back pain, and clotting factors rise while venous return slows, so venous thrombosis is more likely, above all after birth.

Labour is a positive feedback loop: the myometrium gains oxytocin receptors near term, prostaglandins efface the cervix, and pressure of the baby's head releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which strengthens the contractions until birth. Labour has three stages: dilatation of the cervix, the birth itself, and delivery of the placenta, which ends with the uterus clamping its spiral arteries to limit bleeding. Prolactin then makes milk and oxytocin ejects it, the uterus involutes over about six weeks, and pelvic floor muscle training is advised. The same physiology applies to anyone with a uterus and ovaries, including trans men and non-binary people. Some changes are warnings: severe headache, visual disturbance, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a painful calf, vaginal bleeding or reduced fetal movements mean contacting a midwife or maternity unit the same day, and chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting or heavy bleeding need emergency care.

sex-hormones.name: Sex hormones and puberty
sex-hormones.summary: Oestradiol, progesterone and testosterone are steroid hormones made mainly by the ovaries and testes under the control of the hypothalamus and pituitary; they drive puberty, maintain the reproductive organs and act on bone, muscle, fat, skin, blood and brain throughout life.
body: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis controls the sex hormones. The hypothalamus releases gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in pulses and the pituitary answers with luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). In the ovaries FSH drives follicle growth and oestradiol, while LH supports the corpus luteum and its progesterone; in the testes LH drives testosterone and FSH supports sperm production. Inhibin from the gonads suppresses FSH, and the sex steroids feed back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary; the one exception is the sustained mid-cycle rise in oestradiol, which switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge that causes ovulation. Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) from small growing follicles is used as a marker of how many follicles remain.

All of them are steroids made from cholesterol that pass into cells and bind nuclear receptors, the oestrogen, androgen and progesterone receptors, switching genes on or off over hours to days. Both sexes make both hormones: adult men have much higher testosterone and adult women have higher oestradiol for most of the cycle, and men make oestradiol mainly by converting testosterone with the enzyme aromatase. Aromatase is also active in adipose tissue, which is the main source of oestrogen after the menopause. Oestrogen promotes bone density and closes the growth plates in both sexes, so bone is lost when it falls at the menopause; androgens build muscle and strength, stimulate red cell production and, as dihydrotestosterone (DHT), drive body hair and male-pattern hair loss. Progesterone from the corpus luteum turns the proliferative endometrium into a secretory lining ready for implantation, raises basal body temperature by a few tenths of a degree and, if pregnancy follows, holds the pregnancy until the placenta takes over.

Puberty has two parts. Adrenarche, from about the age of six to eight, is the adrenal glands beginning to make androgens, which later give pubic and underarm hair. Gonadarche follows when the GnRH pulses reawaken and LH and FSH rise: in girls puberty normally begins between 8 and 13, the first sign being breast budding, followed by pubic hair, the growth spurt and a first period about two years later; in boys it normally begins between 9 and 14 with enlargement of the testes, then penile growth, pubic hair, voice deepening and a later growth spurt. Clinicians stage these changes with the Tanner scale, from 1 to 5. Oestrogen, made from testosterone in boys, contributes to the growth spurt alongside testosterone and growth hormone, and is what finally fuses the epiphyseal plates. This is the usual course of puberty in people assigned female or male at birth; gender-affirming hormone therapy produces a different set of changes, and puberty in trans and non-binary young people is managed by specialist services.

Levels are not fixed. Testosterone peaks in the morning, so it is sampled then; oestradiol is lowest in the early follicular phase and highest just before ovulation; progesterone rises only after ovulation, so a mid-luteal sample confirms that ovulation happened. Oestradiol falls and FSH rises at the menopause. A result is read with LH and FSH and with the timing of the sample: a low sex steroid with high LH and FSH points to the gonad, one with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH to the hypothalamus or pituitary. This is the axis that hormonal contraception, hormone replacement therapy and gender-affirming hormone therapy act on.
